summary.text: Take \(n=0\). Since \(\Phi_1(0)=-1\) and every cyclotomic polynomial \(\Phi_k\) with \(k>1\) has constant term \(1\), the absolute value of \(\Phi_k(0)\) is always \(1\), hence never prime.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\Phi_k(x)\) denote the \(k\)-th cyclotomic polynomial. The formal statement under consideration quantifies over every natural number \(n\), with natural numbers including \(0\), and asserts that there is a positive integer \(k\) for which
\[
  \bigl|\Phi_k(n)\bigr|
\]
is prime. We disprove this universal statement by taking \(n=0\).

Suppose, toward a contradiction, that the assertion were true. Applying it at \(n=0\), there would be a natural number \(k>0\) such that
\[
  \bigl|\Phi_k(0)\bigr|
\]
is prime. We consider all possible positive values of \(k\).

First suppose \(k=1\). The first cyclotomic polynomial is
\[
  \Phi_1(x)=x-1.
\]
Consequently,
\[
  \Phi_1(0)=0-1=-1,
\]
and hence
\[
  \bigl|\Phi_1(0)\bigr|=|-1|=1.
\]
But \(1\) is not prime, contradicting the required primality.

It remains to consider \(k\ne 1\). Since \(k\) is a positive natural number, \(k\ne1\) implies \(k>1\). For every cyclotomic polynomial of index greater than one, the constant coefficient is \(1\):
\[
  [x^0]\Phi_k(x)=1 \qquad (k>1).
\]
Evaluation of a polynomial at zero selects precisely its constant coefficient. Therefore
\[
  \Phi_k(0)=[x^0]\Phi_k(x)=1.
\]
It follows again that
\[
  \bigl|\Phi_k(0)\bigr|=|1|=1,
\]
which is not prime. This also contradicts the required primality.

Thus neither possible case for a positive \(k\)—namely \(k=1\) or \(k>1\)—can produce a prime value at \(n=0\). Equivalently,
\[
  \forall k\in\mathbb N,\quad k>0\Longrightarrow
  \bigl|\Phi_k(0)\bigr|=1,
\]
so no qualifying \(k\) exists for \(n=0\). Hence the statement
\[
  \forall n\in\mathbb N\;\exists k\in\mathbb N,
  \quad k>0\ \text{and}\ \bigl|\Phi_k(n)\bigr|\text{ is prime}
\]
is false.

This disproof depends essentially on the formal statement allowing \(n=0\). If “positive integer \(n\)” is instead interpreted as requiring \(n\ge1\), then \(0\) is outside the domain, and the argument above does not refute that differently quantified version of the conjecture.
